title: Color a Three-Wide Strip
statement:
A strip of tiles has n rows and exactly 3 columns. Every tile gets one of 3 colors. Two tiles that share a side, in the same row or in the same column, must have different colors.

Return the number of valid colorings. The number grows fast, so return it modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: A single row: 3 choices for the first tile, 2 for the middle, 2 for the last.
Not 12 · 12. Each first row allows only some second rows: 5 for a row like red-green-red, 4 for a row like red-green-blue.
The count per row keeps depending on which kind of row came before, so it is not a fixed multiple of 54.

hints: Only the previous row matters for which rows can come next. How many valid single rows are there?
There are 12 valid rows. You can run a DP over them: for each row pattern, the number of strips ending in it. The step from one row to the next only checks the three columns.
Group the 12 rows into two kinds: two colors like A-B-A (6 rows) and three colors like A-B-C (6 rows). Below an A-B-A row fit 3 A-B-A rows and 2 A-B-C rows; below an A-B-C row fit 2 of each.

explain.intuition:
Rows only interact with their neighbours, so build the strip row by row and remember just the last row. A single row has 12 valid colorings, and a DP that counts "strips of height k ending in row pattern p" already works: 12 states, 144 checks per row.

Symmetry shrinks it to two numbers. Every valid row is either an A-B-A row (outer tiles match) or an A-B-C row (all three differ), 6 of each. Since renaming colors does not change how many rows fit underneath, all A-B-A rows behave the same, and so do all A-B-C rows. Counting by hand: under an A-B-A row fit 3 A-B-A rows and 2 A-B-C rows; under an A-B-C row fit 2 of each. So aba' = 3·aba + 2·abc and abc' = 2·aba + 2·abc, starting from 6 and 6.
steps: Start with aba = 6, abc = 6 for the first row.
Repeat n − 1 times: newAba = (3·aba + 2·abc) mod M, newAbc = (2·aba + 2·abc) mod M.
Take the modulo after every step so the numbers stay small.
pitfalls: Treating rows as independent and answering 12 · 9ⁿ⁻¹ or similar. How many rows fit below depends on the kind of row above.
Forgetting the vertical rule, or the horizontal one, when listing the 12 rows or the transitions between them.
Taking the modulo only at the end. In JavaScript the numbers lose precision long before n = 5000.

solutions.title: DP over the 12 row patterns
solutions.idea: List all valid rows. For each new row, sum the counts of every previous row that differs from it in all three columns.

solutions.title: Two kinds of rows
solutions.idea: A-B-A rows and A-B-C rows each behave alike. Track one count per kind with the fixed transition 3/2 and 2/2.

followups: Solve it for n up to 10¹⁸. (Hint: the two-state step is a 2×2 matrix.)
What changes with 4 colors, or with 4 columns instead of 3?
